ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • Progressive reduction in hearing and facial numbness on the left side; no clear precipitating event.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset ≈ 3 weeks ago, gradual worsening. Numbness is constant; hearing decline persistent.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Hearing: Left-sided decreased acuity; intermittent left-sided tinnitus.  
  • Vestibular: Occasional dizziness temporally related to tinnitus.  
  • Facial sensation: Left jawline/peri-auricular numbness.  
  • NO throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling.  
  • NO nasal/ocular allergy symptoms (nasal polyps stable).  
  • NO stridor/noisy breathing or dyspnea.  
  • NO visible/subjective swelling of lips, tongue, uvula, or face.  
  • NO ear pain, discharge, pruritus, or fever.  
  • NO limb weakness, swallowing or speech difficulty, or visual changes.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Remote episode labelled “labyrinthitis.”  
  • Chronic nasal polyps – uses intranasal spray PRN.  
  • No previous similar neuro-otologic episodes, no prior ED visits/hospitalizations for this issue.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergy: Latex.  
  • Medications: Intranasal spray for polyps (name/dose/frequency not documented, PRN); OTC antacid (Rennie, PRN).
- Social context:
  • 40-year-old female jockey; lives with partner; no pets; currently limiting training due to dizziness.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported/visualized.
- Airway/breathing: No distress noted via video; normal speech.
- Mental status: Alert, appropriate; anxiety about seriousness expressed.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (video consultation only).
- Accompaniment: Patient at home; partner not on call.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Unilateral (left) sensorineural hearing loss with concurrent left facial numbness – requires in-person neuro-otologic and cranial-nerve examination today.
  • Preliminary clinical thought (per treating clinician): possible Bell’s palsy, but physical exam needed.
- Evidence summary:
  • 3-week progressive unilateral hearing deficit, tinnitus, facial numbness.  
  • Negative for otalgia, rash, systemic symptoms, or other cranial-nerve deficits on history.
- Differential diagnosis (selected from DDx consistent with transcript):
  1. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) – fits unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial sensory change; family history of neurofibromatosis strengthens consideration. Opposing: relatively short 3-week course.
  2. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – suggested by clinician; unilateral facial sensory change without systemic signs. Opposing: sensory (not motor) deficit predominant; associated hearing loss atypical; subacute onset.
  3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome – compatible with unilateral auditory symptoms but lacks ear pain or vesicular rash (opposing evidence).
  (Conflict noted: clinician favors Bell’s palsy; DDx ranks vestibular schwannoma higher.)

Plan:
- Immediate arrangements:
  • Same-day face-to-face clinic appointment for full cranial-nerve and otoscopic examination, hearing assessment, and neurological evaluation; booking facilitated through support line within 5 minutes.
- Patient instructions:
  • Attend scheduled clinic today; bring any current medications.  
  • Seek urgent care (call emergency services) if new weakness, worsening dizziness, severe headache, vision changes, or sudden escalation of hearing loss occur before appointment.
- Follow-up:
  • Post-clinic: anticipate need for formal audiogram and possible MRI internal auditory meatus/C-P angle if exam suggests retro-cochlear pathology.  
  • ENT and/or neurology referral based on in-person findings.  
  • Continue intranasal spray as needed; no new medications started today.
- Education/reassurance:
  • Clinician advised condition unlikely to be immediately life-threatening; further assessment needed for definitive diagnosis.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements:
  – Objective cranial-nerve and otoscopic examination, audiogram, imaging, vital signs.  
  – Detailed medication name/dose for intranasal steroid.  
  – Complete allergy list (only latex documented).  
  – Review of cardiovascular risk factors and recent head/ear trauma history.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  – Treating clinician’s provisional diagnosis (Bell’s palsy) vs DDx highest-ranked vestibular schwannoma; uncertainty acknowledged.
● Transcript quality:
  – Clear and audible; minor conversational fillers; no significant data loss.
